reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a bot with a daily profit claim and reports approximately 0.3 Ethereum in profit as connected to the bot's operation. It directs viewers to deploy the contract, send 1 Ether to it, and activate automated buying and selling, while also claiming a 175~180% better return tied to a 1.5 ETH deposit.

citations.quote: I want to share with you the front-run smart contract bot that I recently developed. That can help you make large amounts of profit within a short amount of time.

The bot then places the buy order in the same block, which pumps the market slightly. The bot then waits for the identified transaction to come through, which executes at a higher price and pumps the market even more. The bot then places the sell order and makes easy profits.

Select Injected Web 3 as the environment. And then Metamask will ask you for confirmation to connect your wallet to Remix. Click on the Next and Connect buttons in the Metamask pop-up window. Then click on the Deploy button and confirm the signature in Metamask.
Let's go to the wallet and send some funds to the contract that we just created. I'm going to start with 1 Ether.
After it's sent to the contract and pressing the action button, the bot automatically starts. Buying and selling for you.

opening.argument: Judge, the funding guidance acknowledges costs that can reduce the amount available to trade. The creator says viewers had failed to account for gas and possible burn fees, and gives an example in which a token's burn fee takes 0.1 ETH from 1.0 ETH. The suggested minimum is framed as a recommendation for the bot to work properly, not a promise that every deposit will earn a return. Those qualifications matter when interpreting the profit claim.

citations.quote: I got messages from people who didn't fund enough to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.
If it targets tokens with 10% burn, that's another 0.1 ETH taken off of 1.0 ETH.
So in order for the bot to work properly, I recommend you to fund at least 1.0 ETH.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited deployment and funding steps establish that viewers are shown how to operate a contract, but those steps alone do not establish what the contract ultimately does with their funds. Nor does the creator's explanation of a possible trading sequence establish that it succeeds reliably. The description explicitly identifies costs that can diminish the funds available, a qualification the opening leaves out.

citations.quote: Let's go to the wallet and send some funds to the contract that we just created. I'm going to start with 1 Ether.
I got messages from people who didn't fund enough to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A warning about fees does not neutralize the solicitation. The video tells viewers to fund the contract and activate automated trading, while the description recommends increasing the deposit to 1.5 ETH on the basis of a claimed better return. The cited caveats concern costs, not whether the advertised profit mechanism works or whether deposited funds can be recovered.

citations.quote: After it's sent to the contract and pressing the action button, the bot automatically starts. Buying and selling for you.
the current Bot v2 with 1.5 ETH deposit earns up to 175~180% better return than the old Bot v1 generation (with 1.0 ETH deposit)

opening.argument: Judge, the presentation is structured as a Solidity walkthrough: create a contract file, paste code, select a compiler, deploy, and inspect the resulting contract. The speaker narrates a reported result in the first person rather than furnishing independent proof of returns for every viewer. That leaves room to read the video primarily as an operational demonstration of a claimed bot, even if its trading explanation and result deserve skepticism.

citations.quote: Go to the sidebar on the left and create a new contract under contracts folder. We're going to name it bot.
Click on the compile bot.sol button and wait
Great so the contract is created.
So I made around 0.3 Ethereum of profit.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the narrated profit and funding instructions as decisive. But the cited wallet-connection sequence is also a normal part of the demonstrated deployment workflow, and the account of buying and selling describes how the speaker says the bot works; neither quote verifies that the contract produces those trades. A narrated example should be distinguished from proof of its outcome.

citations.quote: Select Injected Web 3 as the environment. And then Metamask will ask you for confirmation to connect your wallet to Remix.
The bot then places the sell order and makes easy profits.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is also an invitation to reproduce a funded profit scheme. Viewers are directed to send funds to the newly created contract and activate it; the speaker then attributes a profit and withdrawal to that process. Calling the sequence a demonstration does not remove its promotional claim or the requested deposit.

citations.quote: Let's go to the wallet and send some funds to the contract that we just created. I'm going to start with 1 Ether.
To activate the contract, just press the action button and confirm the transaction.
Yep, I've got my balance plus the profit the bot made for me.

opening.argument: Judge, the observed transaction is described as funding a contract the viewer deploys, not paying the presenter for access to a service. The description says deployment makes it 'your own BOT,' and the speaker directs viewers to check that the contract appears on Etherscan before funding it. The supplied material does not itself show a transfer to the presenter's wallet, a request for account credentials, or a commission for recruiting others. Those missing links matter before treating this as a demonstrated diversion of viewers' money.

citations.quote: After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
So now we need to make sure that our contract shows up in Etherscan.
Let's go to the wallet and send some funds to the contract that we just created.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The other side establishes that the presenter urges deployment, funding, and activation, but those actions do not by themselves identify the ultimate recipient of contract funds. The presenter describes sending funds to the contract just created and checking that contract on Etherscan. The cited material therefore supports scrutiny of the promised returns, but does not establish a direct payment to the presenter.

citations.quote: Great so the contract is created. The next step in this process is just funding our contract.
So now we need to make sure that our contract shows up in Etherscan.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A direct payment to the presenter is not required for this concern. The video supplies external code for viewers to paste, directs them to deposit funds into the resulting contract, and connects that action to automated trading and profit. Calling it 'your own BOT' does not establish that viewers control where the code can send their funds or that the claimed returns are real.

Deposit funds to exact your BOT contract address
